recA5BnM5umys9yRk.Body: Kyle and Serena Denton are community herbalists creating wild-crafted and organic plant medicines out of Milwaukee since 2015. I have used their teas and tinctures on an almost daily basis for years now. Kyle is a great friend of InnerVerse and has appeared on the channel more times than I can count. These products work—not in the allopathic "pharma-medicine" way, but in a terrain-support, consciousness bolstering plant-teacher sort of way.

recABS9cTyYGHFXEG.Body: The Sonic Slider is the flagship tool behind Biofield Tuning itself, a weighted tuning fork hand-tuned to 93.96 Hz, the twelfth harmonic of the Schumann Resonance, Earth's own natural electromagnetic pulse. Its extended handle lets you glide it smoothly across the face, neck, and body, and practitioners and users regularly report support for relaxation, circulation, and nervous system regulation. It's the same fork Chance uses in his own sessions, and a great entry point if you want to bring this work into your own daily routine.
recABS9cTyYGHFXEG.Name: The Sonic Slider

recFdBmTf1pJJOP6S.Body: LotusWei provides amazing and transformative plant essence elixirs, using one of nature's most gentle and beautiful elements—the flowers themselves. Led by founder Katie Hess, LotusWei supports customers with diverse products that operate on homeopathic principles and energetic resonances. I use LotusWei Elixirs to give me an edge with psychic & energetic sensitivity, discernment, and life force coherence. In other words, LotusWei Elixirs help me be a better podcaster and Biofield Tuner. Benefits accumulate over long term use!

recMVdJjP2VZJyI2m.Body: Clive de Carle has spent decades researching high-quality natural health essentials, from magnesium and fulvic minerals to iodine, selenium, and vegan-sourced vitamin D. His supplements are formulated with a focus on bioavailability, so the body can actually absorb and use what you're taking rather than letting it pass through unused. It's a simple, no-nonsense approach to filling the nutritional gaps most modern diets leave behind.
recMVdJjP2VZJyI2m.Name: Clive de Carle

rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Bio: Chance Garton is the host and producer of the Innerverse Podcast, where for over a decade he has investigated consciousness, mythology, symbolism, terrain health, and the psychosomatic language of the human body and mind. A biofield tuning practitioner, he uses tuning forks to help clients resolve physical symptoms, break negative patterns, and return to energetic coherence.
rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Name: Chance Garton
rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Role: Host of the Innerverse Podcast, biofield tuning practitioner & researcher

recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Bio: Kyle Denton is a community herbalist and medicine maker from Wisconsin who founded Tippecanoe Herbs with his wife Serena Marinelli in 2015. From their Milwaukee apothecary they craft small batch remedies from locally harvested and organic herbs, working from a bio terrain philosophy that blends Ayurveda with Western herbalism. He also runs Root Radical Herbal Academy, has taught for over a decade through his annual three season class and his Milwaukee herb walks, and sees clients as the Tuning Herbalist, using tuning forks to read the biofield. His Substack and podcast, Resonature, explore the interval between vital herbalism, biofield tuning and cosmology.
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Name: Kyle Denton
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Role: Community herbalist, founder of Tippecanoe Herbs

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Teaching Yourself to Tune", "body": "Kyle Denton describes learning biofield tuning by doing it. Rather than screenshot Chance's slides from Vibe Rant 111, he paused the episode, took notes and drew his own chart of what goes where, then set up a raised table with a six foot piece of cardboard marked with a chalk outline of a body and a rotating cast of stones and crystals. He credits Chance and Eileen Day McKusick as mentors, says his first remote session was over FaceTime with his wife upstairs, and suggests beginning on a best friend, a spouse or a dog. Chance argues the whole method is already public and self teachable."}, {"title": "Clearing the Story, Not Just the Static", "body": "Chance explains a shift in his own practice, from sweeping stuck energy to hunting the story behind it. He recounts a client whose back left sacral, solar plexus and heart work ended with a rush of energy in a right knee he never put a fork near, and describes the back left heart as the zone of feeling drained by others, where the useful move is naming the noble motive behind a victim posture before showing the program underneath. Kyle compares it to bodyworkers who ask a knot to release rather than ironing it out, and says he resists calling himself a healer."}, {"title": "Herbal Formulas Built on the Tuning Table", "body": "Kyle calls this his own contribution to the art. He keeps roughly 25 working herbs out of the 250 or so at his Tippecanoe Herbs shop, sets a plant on the energy center it matches, and as he sweeps the fork he combs that energy back into the herb: chamomile with its yellow and white at the solar plexus, deep green skullcap at the heart. He usually builds with four herbs, sweeps the piles together, grinds them, runs them through a percolation cone with alcohol, then ships the result or bags it as a tea. Asked to name one plant, he picks yarrow, Achillea millefolium."}, {"title": "Tarot and I Ching as Practitioner Tools", "body": "Chance says tarot is how he narrows a general biofield zone down to one person's actual story, walking through a two of discs pulled on a guilt and shame reading, and calls the cards training wheels that became less necessary as the insight started arriving directly. Kyle joins in with his Herb Crafters Tarot, drawing the sun and St. John's wort for a hypothetical client who cannot say no. They then read live for listeners: horsetail and the ten of earth with hexagram 59, dispersion, for Marty, ginger and the eight of fire for Rachel, and yucca with hexagram 36 for Gabe."}, {"title": "The Oak, the Druids and the Acorn", "body": "Revisiting his Root Radical herb of the week, Kyle builds a case around the oak: the botanical name Quercus, the Celtic duir for oak that he links to the word door and to druid, and Godfrey Higgins' book Celtic Druids. He describes the oak as a tree said to tempt lightning and to mark reservoirs of water underground, sacred to lightning gods and read as Thor's tree. Chance adds that the Celtic healing god Bellanus echoes the Greek balanos for acorn. Kyle then covers balanophagy, leaching tannins from acorn meal to make flour, and the oak king dethroned by the holly king."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Our most esteemed herbalist and wizard Kyle Denton joins Vibe Rant tonight for a casual Q & A session. We'll talk about his journey of discovery with adding Biofield Tuning to his healing toolkit, his recent research on the symbolic treasure trove of the oak tree, have some fun banter, and field questions from the audience! Guaranteed to be the best VIBES you'll find online tonight!
